Hand-drawn ink illustration layered over Leonardo source material: Vitruvian Man in clouds, St Peter's dome with perspective construction lines, the Mona Lisa merged into a horizon with a rider silhouette, notebook mirror-script behind a portrait
Each frame is a distinct composite with its own scale and subject. Close-ups (hand, face) alternate with wide landscapes, which suggests real choreography rather than one repeated layout
Rich layering of paper grain, ink spatter, glow and smoke, with a consistent desaturated violet/umber grade across every frame
Credits are set in small-caps serif and placed inside each composition; the role/name hierarchy is handled properly
Weaknesses: the type is tasteful but conventional period-drama dressing, and the 'sketchbook comes alive' concept is the expected route for a Da Vinci subject
gaps: Find one governing visual idea, as B does with the spiral/eye, instead of a montage of Leonardo's greatest hits; the frames read as a collage of references more than a single argument
Give the typography its own point of view (scale, a custom period face, interaction with the drawn lines) rather than discreet small-caps captions
Push the palette past the generic 'aged parchment + purple grade' toward a bolder, ownable colour idea

tells: A single, specific idea that only this film could have: vertigo and obsession expressed as spirographic forms spiralling out of an extreme close-up of a woman's eye
A deliberate, unusual palette: monochrome red-washed photography against black fields with magenta and acid-green Lissajous forms
Typography with real character: an outlined slab/Clarendon display face for the title and director, and a stacked, right-aligned credit block that balances the spiral mass
Clear choreography: eye → spiral emerging from the pupil → abstract forms rotating and morphing in colour → a return to the eye. It is a bookended structure, not a slideshow
Every frame works as a poster, and the generative forms carry live photographic and mechanical texture rather than reading as a digital default
gaps: Benchmark entry. The only quibbles are the dense credit block in frame 4, which crowds the spiral
Mid-sequence the black voids feel slightly sparse next to the bookend photography
The light/texture work is limited by its era compared with modern compositing

tells: A specific concept: early-80s computing seen as a macro journey through circuitry, scan lines and silicon, ending in the title glowing like an overheating core
A bold, near-monochrome red/magenta palette held throughout with real tonal range, from hot pink fields to deep oxblood
Real light and texture: glitch striation, horizontal light streaks, a photographed die with caustic glow, a vignetted bloom on the title card
Typography contrast that carries meaning: a delicate Garamond-style serif for credits against a wide-tracked bold sans title with a pixel-block glyph, which nods to the hardware
Varied frame structure (abstract glitch, silhouette portrait, overhead chip grid, horizon streak, macro object, title) implies choreographed shifts in scale and pacing
gaps: The glitch vocabulary is now widely imitated, so it needs one more unexpected image (like B's eye-to-spiral transformation) to be unforgettable
Integrate the credits with the imagery, for example credits behaving like signal or data, rather than sitting as a serif overlay in the lower third
Tighten the mid-sequence frames (the four-square chip, the horizon streak), which are less poster-like than the opener and the title card

tells: Hand-drawn ink illustration layered over Leonardo's notebook pages and mirror-script, with codex material used as the image itself rather than as decoration
Real texture throughout: ink spatter, parchment grain, smoky cloud plates, and a bruised violet-umber palette held consistently across frames

Every frame is built differently (Vitruvian figure in clouds, St Peter's with perspective lines, quill close-up, Mona Lisa as landscape, upturned portrait inside an orbit arc, the flying-machine rider), which suggests a camera travelling through one illustrated world
Layered depth, with figure, diagram and ground in separate planes
gaps: Typography is a conventional small-caps serif credit placed in open space; unlike B, the type never becomes part of the idea or the image
The metaphor ('genius sketches the world') is apt but expected for a Leonardo series; it needs a single sharp graphic conceit like B's spiral
Grunge overlays and painterly filters date it and occasionally muddy the read; reduce them to one or two decisive textures

tells: A single idea that belongs only to this film: the vertigo spiral comes out of a human eye, so the title sequence enacts the film's obsession
Extreme scale contrast, from a macro eye filling the frame to a black void holding mathematical Lissajous/spirograph forms
Bold slab-serif display face with an outline treatment, set in hierarchical credit stacks with small labels and large names; the type has a voice and sits on the image (VERTIGO across the eye)
Unusual, deliberate palette: monochrome blood-red film plate against magenta and then acid-green line forms on black
Choreography is legible across frames: eye → spiral emerges in the pupil → forms rotate and morph in the void → back to the eye for the director credit, a closed loop
Every frame works as a poster
gaps: Benchmark entry; the gaps are minor
Some credit blocks are dense and right-ragged against the forms; tighter integration of type with the spirals' motion would elevate them further
Colour shifts between spirals are abrupt rather than motivated

tells: Clear conceptual spine: early-computing signal and glitch, the title's 'halt and catch fire' machine instruction rendered as overheating silicon ending in a burning red disc
Bold near-monochrome palette of hot red/magenta, used as an emotional temperature that rises across the sequence
Mixed media: scanline and datamosh textures, silhouettes of cast in the noise, macro photography of a glowing die in a liquid dish, and a 2x2 pixel/chip grid as a graphic motif
Variety of frame structures with real light (bloom, specular, glow) and a progression from abstraction to object to fire
gaps: Credit typography is a fairly default transitional serif in light weight; only the end title (blocky square glyph + tracked caps) shows a typographic idea
Glitch-as-tech is a widely used visual language; the piece needs a moment of surprise beyond 'signal breaks down'
Some frames (the horizontal light streak) are near-effect-without-subject; anchor each beat to a concrete object as B does with the eye

defects: Long stretches of near-empty sky (0-3s, and the frame-3 region): a few rising tracer ticks on a flat gradient, which is dead air rather than anticipation
There are only 3 shots in 32s, with a 20s unbroken take; the TUESDAY/SATURDAY split screen is a hard divider line with no transition design
The dotted ANIKIT wordmark forms over the dense finale and lands as an illegible red jumble over orange rings before it clears
The headline mask-wipe reveal clips the descenders of 'Same page. Same film.' mid-move, and the wipe is generic
The ring bursts read as stamped-on vector circles. They expand without convincing ballistic deceleration, gravity sag, or a decaying trail, and have no glow or light falloff
Willow and pistil fronds are uniform-weight strokes with no taper or fade, so they look like plotted lines rather than spent embers
In the end card, the JSON spec text block, the logo, the URL and 'Anikit Video' compete; the hierarchy is cramped in the lower-right quadrant
Audio drops to near-silence at about 18-20s. It works as a pre-finale breath, but the fade is a plain lowpass roll-off rather than a designed riser or suck-back
gaps: Pacing and choreography: build sequenced bursts, cuts or camera moves that hand off every 1-2s, with real anticipation (a launch trail that leads the eye) and overshoot/settle on each bloom, instead of long held wide shots of sparse sky

Material and light: give bursts a hot core, additive glow, sky illumination, ember decay with tapered trails, and gravity on falling sparks. At 100% the work is flat vector on grain, and there's no sense of light or air

Sound design: the noise-burst cracks and sparse tonal partials sync to bursts, but the bed is thin and static. Missing are layered low-end thumps, distance delay/reverb tails, crackle textures, and a score that crescendoes into the finale and resolves on the logo
